claim: Reef-building corals depend on intracellular dinoflagellate symbionts that provide nutrients.
source: Reef-building corals depend on intracellular dinoflagellate symbionts that provide nutrients.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in coral biology, supported by extensive literature and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The transfer of sterols is essential for corals and other sterol-auxotrophic cnidarians.
source: Besides sugars, the transfer of sterols is essential for corals and other sterol-auxotrophic cnidarians.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous work.

claim: Variants of the conserved Niemann-Pick Type C2 (NPC2) sterol transporter are vastly up-regulated in symbiotic cnidarians.
source: Sterols are important cell components, and variants of the conserved Niemann-Pick Type C2 (NPC2) sterol transporter are vastly up-regulated in symbiotic cnidarians.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both symbiont- and host-driven patterns of sterol transfer are observed in different pairings of symbiont strains with lines of Aiptasia anemones or Acropora corals.
source: Using different pairings of symbiont strains with lines of Aiptasia anemones or Acropora corals, we observe both symbiont- and host-driven patterns of sterol transfer, revealing plasticity of sterol use and functional substitution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Sterol transfer is mediated by the symbiosis-specific, non-canonical NPC2 proteins.
source: We propose that sterol transfer is mediated by the symbiosis-specific, non-canonical NPC2 proteins, which gradually accumulate in the symbiosome.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the immunofluorescence, expression, and binding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2 proteins gradually accumulate in the symbiosome.
source: We propose that sterol transfer is mediated by the symbiosis-specific, non-canonical NPC2 proteins, which gradually accumulate in the symbiosome.
evidence: This is supported by the time-course immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Non-canonical NPCs are adapted to the symbiosome environment, including low pH.
source: Our data suggest that non-canonical NPCs are adapted to the symbiosome environment, including low pH, and play an important role in allowing corals to dominate nutrient-poor shallow tropical seas worldwide.
evidence: This is supported by the protein solubility assays at different pH values shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Non-canonical NPCs play an important role in allowing corals to dominate nutrient-poor shallow tropical seas worldwide.
source: Our data suggest that non-canonical NPCs are adapted to the symbiosome environment, including low pH, and play an important role in allowing corals to dominate nutrient-poor shallow tropical seas worldwide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional importance of sterol transfer demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Cnidarians establish an ecologically critical endosymbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellate algae (family Symbiodiniaceae).
source: Cnidarians, such as reef-building corals and anemones, establish an ecologically critical endosymbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellate algae (Douglas, 2010) (family Symbiodiniaceae) (LaJeunesse et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Symbionts reside within endo/lysosomal-like organelles, termed symbiosomes.
source: Their symbionts reside within endo/lysosomal-like organelles, termed symbiosomes, and transfer photosynthetic products to their hosts (Muscatine, 1990; Yellowlees et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Symbionts transfer photosynthetic products to their hosts.
source: Their symbionts reside within endo/lysosomal-like organelles, termed symbiosomes, and transfer photosynthetic products to their hosts (Muscatine, 1990; Yellowlees et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Recent studies hint at the importance of the transfer of various lipids including sterols.
source: In addition to sugars that mostly provide energy, recent studies hint at the importance of the transfer of various lipids including sterols (Crossland et al., 1980; Battey and Patton, 1984; Revel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sterols are essential building blocks for the cell membrane and endomembrane systems, in the form of cholesterol and other sterol variants.
source: Sterols are essential building blocks for the cell membrane and endomembrane systems, in the form of cholesterol and other sterol variants.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of sterols in cell biology.

claim: Cnidarians are sterol auxotrophs.
source: Cnidarians are sterol auxotrophs (Baumgarten et al., 2015; Gold et al., 2016) that must acquire these essential compounds from diet and/or symbionts (Goad, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cnidarians must acquire sterols from diet and/or symbionts.
source: Cnidarians are sterol auxotrophs (Baumgarten et al., 2015; Gold et al., 2016) that must acquire these essential compounds from diet and/or symbionts (Goad, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and is a logical consequence of being sterol auxotrophs.

claim: Non-canonical variants of the conserved cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick Type C2 (NPC2) are among the most up-regulated genes in symbiotic Exaiptasia pallida and Anemonia viridis anemones.
source: In line with this, non-canonical variants of the conserved cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick Type C2 (NPC2) are among the most up-regulated genes in symbiotic Exaiptasia pallida (commonly Aiptasia) and Anemonia viridis anemones (Dani et al., 2014; Lehnert et al., 2014; Kuo et al., 2010; Ganot et al., 2011; Wolfowicz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Dinoflagellates synthesize various sterols, many of which are found in symbiotic cnidarians.
source: Dinoflagellates synthesize various sterols, many of which are found in symbiotic cnidarians (Bohlin et al., 1981; Withers et al., 1982; Ciereszko, 1989); however, the specific combinations of transferred sterols, as well as the mechanism of this transfer remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The specific combinations of transferred sterols, as well as the mechanism of this transfer remain unknown.
source: Dinoflagellates synthesize various sterols, many of which are found in symbiotic cnidarians (Bohlin et al., 1981; Withers et al., 1982; Ciereszko, 1989); however, the specific combinations of transferred sterols, as well as the mechanism of this transfer remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: For the Aiptasia F003 host line, there is a gradual transition from an initial aposymbiotic, food-derived cholesterol profile to a cholesterol-reduced, algal sterol-enriched symbiotic profile.
source: For the Aiptasia F003 host line, this revealed a gradual transition from an initial aposymbiotic, food-derived cholesterol profile to a cholesterol-reduced, algal sterol-enriched symbiotic profile that was also found in the symbiont-free eggs (and is thus present in host tissue) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The algal sterol-enriched symbiotic profile was also found in the symbiont-free eggs of Aiptasia F003.
source: For the Aiptasia F003 host line, this revealed a gradual transition from an initial aposymbiotic, food-derived cholesterol profile to a cholesterol-reduced, algal sterol-enriched symbiotic profile that was also found in the symbiont-free eggs (and is thus present in host tissue) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sterol composition of coral symbiotic polyps collected from the wild is nearly identical to that of their symbiont-free eggs.
source: We also compared the sterol composition of coral symbiotic polyps collected from the wild to that of their symbiont-free eggs, which again proved nearly identical sterol compositions (Figure 1A) and unambiguously revealed symbiont-to-host tissue transfer.
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Symbiont-derived sterols can functionally replace dietary cholesterol without any further chemical conversion by the host.
source: Taken together, this suggests that symbiont-derived sterols can functionally replace dietary cholesterol without any further chemical conversion by the host.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol profiling data showing that symbiont-derived sterols are present in host tissue.

claim: The sterol content of the hosts is highly plastic.
source: Moreover, the sterol content of the hosts is highly plastic, and sterols are used flexibly as they become available from food and/or symbionts.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of gradual transitions in sterol profiles under different conditions.

claim: Sterols are used flexibly as they become available from food and/or symbionts.
source: Moreover, the sterol content of the hosts is highly plastic, and sterols are used flexibly as they become available from food and/or symbionts.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of gradual transitions in sterol profiles under different conditions.

claim: Aiptasia CC7 hosting Symbiodiniaceae strain SSA01 contained a large proportion of stigmasterol-like sterol when compared to campesterol.
source: We found that Aiptasia CC7 hosting Symbiodiniaceae strain SSA01 contained a large proportion of stigmasterol-like sterol (dark blue, Figure 1B) when compared to campesterol (light blue, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The same Aiptasia line CC7 hosting strain SSB01 contained minimal stigmasterol-like derivatives compared to campesterol, as well as the unique sterol gorgosterol.
source: In contrast, the same Aiptasia line hosting strain SSB01 contained minimal stigmasterol-like derivatives compared to campesterol, as well as the unique sterol gorgosterol (light blue and pink, respectively, Figure 1B), characterized by an unusual cyclopropyl group (Ciereszko, 1989). (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gorgosterol is characterized by an unusual cyclopropyl group.
source: In contrast, the same Aiptasia line hosting strain SSB01 contained minimal stigmasterol-like derivatives compared to campesterol, as well as the unique sterol gorgosterol (light blue and pink, respectively, Figure 1B), characterized by an unusual cyclopropyl group (Ciereszko, 1989). (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A very similar sterol profile was observed when the same symbiont (SSB01) infected the H2 host line, indicating that the host sterol profile was largely symbiont-driven.
source: A very similar sterol profile was observed when the same symbiont (SSB01) infected the H2 host line, indicating that the host sterol profile was largely symbiont-driven.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of sterol profiles in different host-symbiont pairings shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Aiptasia line F003 hosting both SSA01 and SSB01, the sterol proportions reflect both symbionts: a dominance of stigmasterol-like sterol (reflecting SSA01) together with gorgosterol (reflecting SSB01).
source: Likewise, in Aiptasia line F003 hosting both SSA01 and SSB01, the sterol proportions reflect both symbionts: a dominance of stigmasterol-like sterol (reflecting SSA01) together with gorgosterol (reflecting SSB01) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sterol profile of Acropora colonies collected from the wild shows a strong enrichment for gorgosterol and campesterol at the expense of stigmasterol-like sterols.
source: We also compared the sterol profile of Acropora colonies collected from the wild to that of a closely related symbiont CCMP2466 in laboratory culture and found a strong enrichment for gorgosterol and campesterol at the expense of stigmasterol-like sterols – highly reminiscent of the trend previously observed in the SSB01/CC7 and SSB01/H2 pairings (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two major patterns of sterol transfer were observed in symbiont-host combinations – one enriching for stigmasterol-like sterols and another one enriching for gorgosterol and campesterol.
source: We thus observed two major patterns of sterol transfer in our symbiont-host combinations – one enriching for stigmasterol-like sterols (combinations SSA01/CC7 and SSA01 +SSB01/F003), and another one enriching for gorgosterol and campesterol (combinations SSB01/CC7; SSB01/H2; and CCMP2466/Acropora).
evidence: This is a summary of the sterol profiling data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Selective sterol transfer and/or accumulation by the host may occur.
source: This suggests that selective sterol transfer and/or accumulation by the host may occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of sterol transfer.

claim: Certain sterols were absent in symbiont-enriched pellets yet present in symbiont cultures.
source: This revealed that certain sterols were absent in symbiont-enriched pellets yet present in symbiont cultures (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Stigmasterol/gorgosterol-like and ergost-tetrol-like sterol are proportionally highly abundant in cultured symbionts, yet are basically absent in all pellet samples.
source: For example, stigmasterol/gorgosterol-like (dark purple) and ergost-tetrol-like sterol (light purple) are proportionally highly abundant in cultured symbionts, yet are basically absent in all pellet samples (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sterol profiling data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Synthesis of at least some sterols changes in residence vs. in culture.
source: This suggests that synthesis of at least some sterols changes in residence vs. in culture, providing further support that the symbiont has a major influence on which specific composition and proportion of the sterols are transferred during symbiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of sterol profiles in cultured symbionts vs. symbionts in symbiosis.

claim: The symbiont has a major influence on which specific composition and proportion of the sterols are transferred during symbiosis.
source: This suggests that synthesis of at least some sterols changes in residence vs. in culture, providing further support that the symbiont has a major influence on which specific composition and proportion of the sterols are transferred during symbiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol profiling data.

claim: Cultured symbionts exhibited some degree of plasticity of sterol profiles under various culturing conditions.
source: Further, cultured symbionts exhibited some degree of plasticity of sterol profiles under various culturing conditions (e.g. SSA01 in Figure 1A vs. Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the comparison of sterol profiles shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1C.

claim: The current hypothesis in the field is that non-canonical NPC2s may specifically facilitate transfer of symbiont-produced sterols in cnidarian-algal symbiosis.
source: The current hypothesis in the field is that non-canonical NPC2s may specifically facilitate transfer of symbiont-produced sterols in cnidarian-algal symbiosis (Revel et al., 2016; Baumgarten et al., 2015; Wolfowicz et al., 2016; Dani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanistic analyses of NPC2 function are lacking.
source: However, NPC2s may serve other purposes, for example signaling (Baumgarten et al., 2015; Dani et al., 2017), and mechanistic analyses of NPC2 function are lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Several previously unidentified NPC2 homologues were uncovered in the reef-building corals and other taxa.
source: To characterize them further, we first compared the genomic complement of NPC2 homologues in symbiotic cnidarians to that of non-symbiotic metazoans, uncovering several previously unidentified homologues in the reef-building corals and other taxa (asterisks, Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All canonical NPC2 family members are identified by three shared introns.
source: A Bayesian tree reconstruction placed all canonical NPC2 family members (identified by three shared introns) on a large multifurcation, and all previously and newly identified non-canonical NPC2 (identified by the absence of introns due to retrotransposition [Dani et al., 2014]) to a basal position, most likely attracted by the Capsaspora outgroup NPC2s.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and structural features shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All non-canonical NPC2 are identified by the absence of introns due to retrotransposition.
source: A Bayesian tree reconstruction placed all canonical NPC2 family members (identified by three shared introns) on a large multifurcation, and all previously and newly identified non-canonical NPC2 (identified by the absence of introns due to retrotransposition [Dani et al., 2014]) to a basal position, most likely attracted by the Capsaspora outgroup NPC2s.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s show higher sequence divergence than canonical NPC2s.
source: This indicated higher sequence divergence of non-canonical NPC2s; and in line with this, they contain only around half as many residues under negative (purifying) selection (35 to 61) as canonical NPC2s and twice as many residues under positive (diversifying) selection (12 to 5) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the selection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s contain only around half as many residues under negative (purifying) selection (35 to 61) as canonical NPC2s.
source: This indicated higher sequence divergence of non-canonical NPC2s; and in line with this, they contain only around half as many residues under negative (purifying) selection (35 to 61) as canonical NPC2s and twice as many residues under positive (diversifying) selection (12 to 5) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the selection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s contain twice as many residues under positive (diversifying) selection (12 to 5) as canonical NPC2s.
source: This indicated higher sequence divergence of non-canonical NPC2s; and in line with this, they contain only around half as many residues under negative (purifying) selection (35 to 61) as canonical NPC2s and twice as many residues under positive (diversifying) selection (12 to 5) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the selection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2 homologues are confined to cnidarians within the anthozoan class.
source: Our analysis also revealed that non-canonical NPC2 homologues are confined to cnidarians within the anthozoan class, as they did not appear in the earlier-branching sponge Amphimedon nor in the hydrozoans Hydra magnipapillata and Hydractinia echinata.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The occurrence of non-canonical NPC2s appeared to correlate with symbiotic state.
source: Notably, the occurrence of non-canonical NPC2s appeared to correlate with symbiotic state: the symbiotic anthozoans (Aiptasia, Acropora, Montastrea) have several non-canonical NPC2 homologues (3, 3, and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is an observation based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The symbiotic anthozoans (Aiptasia, Acropora, Montastrea) have several non-canonical NPC2 homologues (3, 3, and 2, respectively).
source: Notably, the occurrence of non-canonical NPC2s appeared to correlate with symbiotic state: the symbiotic anthozoans (Aiptasia, Acropora, Montastrea) have several non-canonical NPC2 homologues (3, 3, and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is directly supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The non-symbiotic anemone Nematostella displays evolutionary traces of a single non-canonical NPC2, which either failed to expand or underwent higher loss.
source: In contrast, the non-symbiotic anemone Nematostella displays evolutionary traces of a single non-canonical NPC2, which either failed to expand or underwent higher loss (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two of the three non-canonical NPC2 homologues in Aiptasia displayed substantially higher expression at the transcript and protein levels in symbiotic but not aposymbiotic animals.
source: As determined by qPCR and Western blotting using custom-made antibodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), two of the three non-canonical NPC2 homologues displayed substantially higher expression at the transcript and protein levels in symbiotic but not aposymbiotic animals (closed blue symbols; Figure 3A+B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The third non-canonical NPC2 homologue in Aiptasia was highly expressed in both symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals, yet more so in symbiotic animals.
source: The third non-canonical NPC2 homologue was highly expressed in both symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals, yet more so in symbiotic animals.
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Canonical NPC2s in Aiptasia were highly expressed in both symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals.
source: Conversely, canonical NPC2s were highly expressed in both symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals (closed red symbols).
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The non-symbiotic anemone Nematostella exhibited ubiquitously high expression of canonical NPC2 genes.
source: Likewise, the non-symbiotic anemone Nematostella exhibited ubiquitously high expression of canonical NPC2 genes (open red symbols), whereas the non-canonical NPC2 gene was highly expressed only upon feeding (open blue symbols).
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The non-canonical NPC2 gene in Nematostella was highly expressed only upon feeding.
source: Likewise, the non-symbiotic anemone Nematostella exhibited ubiquitously high expression of canonical NPC2 genes (open red symbols), whereas the non-canonical NPC2 gene was highly expressed only upon feeding (open blue symbols).
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Aposymbiotic embryos of the symbiotic coral Acropora, as well as Nematostella embryos, contained maternally provided canonical NPC2 transcripts.
source: Aposymbiotic embryos of the symbiotic coral Acropora, as well as Nematostella embryos, contained maternally provided canonical NPC2 transcripts, suggesting that these are required for development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Canonical NPC2 transcripts are required for development.
source: Aposymbiotic embryos of the symbiotic coral Acropora, as well as Nematostella embryos, contained maternally provided canonical NPC2 transcripts, suggesting that these are required for development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of maternally provided transcripts.

claim: Several canonical NPC2s in Aiptasia and Nematostella may be 'in transition' to becoming non-canonical.
source: Notably, several canonical NPC2s in Aiptasia (XM_021046710, XM_021041174) and Nematostella (XM_001635452) may be 'in transition' to becoming non-canonical: they were expressed at intermediate abundances between the two groups, and they responded to symbiosis (Aiptasia) or feeding (Nematostella) (red square and triangles, Figure 3A + 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns and intron/exon structures.

claim: The non-canonical NPC2s decorated intracellular symbionts in Aiptasia in vivo.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the non-canonical NPC2s decorated intracellular symbionts in Aiptasia in vivo (Figure 3C + D), consistent with previous data in Anemonia viridis (Dani et al., 2014; Dani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C and 3D, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The NPC2 signal appears to be restricted to the symbiosome and absent from the cytoplasm of the symbiont-containing cell.
source: The NPC2 signal appears to be restricted to the symbiosome and absent from the cytoplasm of the symbiont-containing cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s decorate some but not all symbionts.
source: We noted that non-canonical NPC2s decorate some but not all symbionts (Dani et al., 2014; Dani et al., 2017), suggesting that at any given time, symbiosomes are a dynamic group of specialized organelles.
evidence: This is an observation based on the immunofluorescence data and previous studies.

claim: At any given time, symbiosomes are a dynamic group of specialized organelles.
source: We noted that non-canonical NPC2s decorate some but not all symbionts (Dani et al., 2014; Dani et al., 2017), suggesting that at any given time, symbiosomes are a dynamic group of specialized organelles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that not all symbionts are decorated with NPC2.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2 slowly decorated intracellular symbionts over time during symbiosis establishment in Aiptasia larvae.
source: Indeed, non-canonical NPC2 slowly decorated intracellular symbionts over time (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the time-course immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Infection rates remained steady after removal of symbionts from the environment, whereas the proportion of larvae showing non-canonical NPC2 signal continued to increase.
source: We found that infection rates remained steady after removal of symbionts from the environment, whereas the proportion of larvae showing non-canonical NPC2 signal continued to increase to eventually include the majority of infected larvae (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The proportion of symbionts within each larva surrounded by NPC2 signal increased over time, as did the signal strength.
source: Concordantly, the proportion of symbionts within each larva surrounded by NPC2 signal also increased over time, as did the signal strength (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Infected larvae displaying any NPC2 signal generally contained a higher symbiont load than their infected, unlabelled counterparts.
source: Finally, infected larvae displaying any NPC2 signal generally contained a higher symbiont load than their infected, unlabelled counterparts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2 is increasingly expressed and recruited to symbionts over time.
source: Thus, non-canonical NPC2 is increasingly expressed and recruited to symbionts over time, suggesting that non-canonical NPC2 function becomes important primarily once symbiosomes become 'mature'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course data.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2 function becomes important primarily once symbiosomes become 'mature'.
source: Thus, non-canonical NPC2 is increasingly expressed and recruited to symbionts over time, suggesting that non-canonical NPC2 function becomes important primarily once symbiosomes become 'mature'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course data.

claim: U18666A is a competitive inhibitor of the NPC2 binding partner NPC1 that is required for efficient cholesterol egress from lysosomes.
source: As a first step towards elucidating NPC2 function during symbiosis, we investigated the effect of global sterol transport inhibition by treating symbiotic and aposymbiotic adult Aiptasia with the drug U18666A, a competitive inhibitor of the NPC2 binding partner NPC1 that is required for efficient cholesterol egress from lysosomes (Liscum and Faust, 1989; Cenedella, 2009; Vance, 2010; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both symbiotic and aposymbiotic anemones appear to lose tissue and shorten their tentacles in a dose- and duration-dependent manner in response to U18666A treatment.
source: Accordingly, we found that both symbiotic and aposymbiotic anemones appear to lose tissue and shorten their tentacles in a dose- and duration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is directly supported by the images shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Symbiotic anemones showed effects on host physiology faster than their aposymbiotic counterparts in response to U18666A treatment.
source: However, symbiotic anemones showed such effects on host physiology faster than their aposymbiotic counterparts (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is directly supported by the images shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Symbiont density decreased in response to U18666A treatment.
source: Moreover, symbiont density decreased in response to U18666A treatment (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Similar effects were observed with A. digitifera juvenile primary polyps stably hosting Symbiodiniaceae strain SSB01 when exposed to increasing concentrations of U18666A.
source: We observed similar effects with A. digitifera juvenile primary polyps stably hosting Symbiodiniaceae strain SSB01 when exposed to increasing concentrations of U18666A (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Inhibition of sterol transport affects symbiosis stability and may lead to loss of symbionts ('bleaching').
source: This suggests that inhibition of sterol transport affects symbiosis stability and may lead to loss of symbionts ('bleaching').
evidence: This is an inference based on the U18666A treatment experiments.

claim: The disruption of global sterol transport compromises host tissues in all cases, emphasizing the importance of sterols in tissue homeostasis.
source: Further, the disruption of global sterol transport compromises host tissues in all cases, emphasizing the importance of sterols in tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the U18666A treatment experiments.

claim: Under both neutral (pH 7) and acidic (pH 5) conditions, canonical and non-canonical NPC2:mCherry fusion proteins bound symbiont-produced sterols significantly above the background levels of the control.
source: Under both conditions, canonical and non-canonical NPC2:mCherry fusion proteins bound symbiont-produced sterols significantly above the background levels of the control, mCherry alone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the lipidomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The relative proportions of bound sterols generally exhibited equilibrium levels with the corresponding symbiont homogenate.
source: The relative proportions of bound sterols generally exhibited equilibrium levels with the corresponding symbiont homogenate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the lipidomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Native non-canonical NPC2 immunoprecipitated from homogenates of symbiotic Aiptasia bound symbiont-produced sterols above background levels.
source: To validate sterol binding by non-canonical NPC2 in vivo, we also immunoprecipitated the native non-canonical NPC2 and bound sterols directly from homogenates of symbiotic Aiptasia. Again, we detected symbiont-produced sterols above background levels, validating our heterologous system and indicating that these proteins bind sterols in vivo during symbiosis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the lipidomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both types of Aiptasia NPC2s have the conserved function of binding sterols in lysosomal-like environments.
source: These data indicate that, despite their evolutionary divergence, both types of Aiptasia NPC2s have the conserved function of binding sterols in lysosomal-like environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol binding assays.

claim: The results suggested no differential binding between canonical and non-canonical NPC2s.
source: Although we cannot rule out subtle differences in sterol binding dynamics between the two proteins, our results suggested no differential binding between canonical and non-canonical NPC2s, consistent with the observations that the sterol ligand and the residues lining the binding cavity tolerate considerable variations (Xu et al., 2007; Liou et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol binding assays and supported by citations.

claim: The sterol ligand and the residues lining the binding cavity tolerate considerable variations.
source: Although we cannot rule out subtle differences in sterol binding dynamics between the two proteins, our results suggested no differential binding between canonical and non-canonical NPC2s, consistent with the observations that the sterol ligand and the residues lining the binding cavity tolerate considerable variations (Xu et al., 2007; Liou et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No difference was detected in the differential expression of canonical and non-canonical NPC2s between aposymbiotic and symbiotic state in three symbiont-Aiptasia pairings.
source: Corroborating this, we were unable to detect any difference in the differential expression of canonical and non-canonical NPC2s between aposymbiotic and symbiotic state in three symbiont-Aiptasia pairings (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mature symbiosomes in steady-state symbiosis are even more acidic (pH ~4) than classic lysosomes to promote efficient photosynthesis.
source: The mature symbiosome, where non-canonical NPC2 appears to function, remains poorly understood; however, extreme acidity appears to be a unique characteristic of these specialized cellular compartments. Whereas lumenal pH of classic lysosomes can range from 4.7 to 6 (Johnson et al., 2016), recent work indicates that mature symbiosomes in steady-state symbiosis are even more acidic (pH ~4) to promote efficient photosynthesis (Barott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lumenal pH of classic lysosomes can range from 4.7 to 6.
source: Whereas lumenal pH of classic lysosomes can range from 4.7 to 6 (Johnson et al., 2016), recent work indicates that mature symbiosomes in steady-state symbiosis are even more acidic (pH ~4) to promote efficient photosynthesis (Barott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The patterns of extracted soluble proteins vary among NPC2s at different pH.
source: Interestingly, the patterns of extracted soluble proteins vary among NPC2s: canonical NPC2 appears in one predominant form at both pH's (Figure 4E, red arrowhead), whereas one of the symbiosis-responsive non-canonical NPC2s (XM_021052412; Figure 3A + B) always appears in two forms in both conditions (Figure 4E, arrowheads and asterisks).
evidence: This is directly supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The pattern for the symbiosis-specific non-canonical NPC2 (XM_021052404) is distinct between pH 7 and pH 5, with a consistently occurring additional band at higher pH.
source: Strikingly, the pattern for the other symbiosis-specific non-canonical NPC2 (XM_021052404; Figures 3A–G and 4A–C) is distinct between pH 7 and pH 5, with a consistently occurring additional band at higher pH (Figure 4E, blue arrow).
evidence: This is directly supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At pH 5, the non-canonical NPC2s were consistently more abundant in the soluble fraction than the canonical counterpart.
source: When quantifying the protein variant common to all samples (Figure 4E, arrowheads), we found that at pH 5, the non-canonical NPC2s were consistently more abundant in the soluble fraction than the canonical counterpart (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: For all proteins tested, the ratio of the predominant soluble protein variant at pH 7 to that at pH 5 was always >1, indicating more solubility at pH 7.
source: For all proteins tested, the ratio of the predominant soluble protein variant at pH 7 to that at pH 5 was always >1, indicating more solubility at pH 7.
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ratio of soluble protein at pH 7 to pH 5 was higher for Aiptasia canonical NPC2 than for the non-canonical NPC2s, indicating that the former is relatively less soluble at pH 5.
source: However, the ratio was higher for Aiptasia canonical NPC2 than for the non-canonical NPC2s, indicating that the former is relatively less soluble at pH 5 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Symbiosis-responsive non-canonical NPC2 appears to be more soluble/stable than canonical NPC2 at a lower pH, likely characteristic of the symbiosome.
source: Taken together, symbiosis-responsive non-canonical NPC2 appears to be more soluble/stable than canonical NPC2 at a lower pH, likely characteristic of the symbiosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protein solubility assays.

claim: All Aiptasia non-canonical NPC2 proteins harbored glycosylation sites and a glycine followed by a histidine residue.
source: In line with this, all Aiptasia non-canonical NPC2 proteins harbored glycosylation sites and a glycine followed by a histidine residue (Figure 2B), which may contribute to protein stability in acidic environments (Rudd et al., 1994; Hanson et al., 2009; Culyba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Glycosylation sites and a glycine followed by a histidine residue may contribute to protein stability in acidic environments.
source: In line with this, all Aiptasia non-canonical NPC2 proteins harbored glycosylation sites and a glycine followed by a histidine residue (Figure 2B), which may contribute to protein stability in acidic environments (Rudd et al., 1994; Hanson et al., 2009; Culyba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The transfer of complex mixtures of symbiont-derived sterols is a key feature of anthozoan photosymbiosis.
source: In summary, our data reveal that the transfer of complex mixtures of symbiont-derived sterols is a key feature of anthozoan photosymbiosis (Figure 4G), whereby the specific composition and proportion of transferred sterols appears to be under the control of both symbiont and host.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The specific composition and proportion of transferred sterols appears to be under the control of both symbiont and host.
source: In summary, our data reveal that the transfer of complex mixtures of symbiont-derived sterols is a key feature of anthozoan photosymbiosis (Figure 4G), whereby the specific composition and proportion of transferred sterols appears to be under the control of both symbiont and host.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol profiling data.

claim: The non-canonical NPC2 sterol-binding proteins are part of the machinery transferring sterols from symbiont to host.
source: While the non-canonical NPC2 sterol-binding proteins are part of the machinery transferring sterols from symbiont to host, they do not contribute to host sterol selection by differential expression or differential binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol binding and expression data.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s do not contribute to host sterol selection by differential expression or differential binding.
source: While the non-canonical NPC2 sterol-binding proteins are part of the machinery transferring sterols from symbiont to host, they do not contribute to host sterol selection by differential expression or differential binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differential expression or binding observed in the experiments.

claim: Ubiquitously expressed canonical NPC2 homologues are 'workhorses' in sterol trafficking throughout the host.
source: We propose that whereas ubiquitously expressed canonical NPC2 homologues are 'workhorses' in sterol trafficking throughout the host, non-canonical NPC2s are spatiotemporally regulated to accumulate as the symbiosome matures, developing into a unique compartment optimized to promote the interaction and communication of the symbiotic partners (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-canonical NPC2s are spatiotemporally regulated to accumulate as the symbiosome matures, developing into a unique compartment optimized to promote the interaction and communication of the symbiotic partners.
source: We propose that whereas ubiquitously expressed canonical NPC2 homologues are 'workhorses' in sterol trafficking throughout the host, non-canonical NPC2s are spatiotemporally regulated to accumulate as the symbiosome matures, developing into a unique compartment optimized to promote the interaction and communication of the symbiotic partners (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Symbiotic cnidarians can flexibly use symbiont-produced sterols.
source: This allows symbiotic cnidarians to flexibly use symbiont-produced sterols, with reef-building corals nearly fully substituting these for prey-derived cholesterol, supporting survival in nutrient-poor environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol profiling data.

claim: Reef-building corals nearly fully substitute symbiont-produced sterols for prey-derived cholesterol, supporting survival in nutrient-poor environments.
source: This allows symbiotic cnidarians to flexibly use symbiont-produced sterols, with reef-building corals nearly fully substituting these for prey-derived cholesterol, supporting survival in nutrient-poor environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterol profiling data showing high proportions of symbiont-derived sterols in corals.

claim: Carbon acquisition by lipid transfer is a major driver of coral-algal symbiotic relationships as a means to adapt to various ecological niches by efficient exploitation of limited resources.
source: More broadly, our findings indicate that carbon acquisition by lipid transfer, similar to other symbioses (Keymer et al., 2017), is a major driver of coral-algal symbiotic relationships as a means to adapt to various ecological niches by efficient exploitation of limited resources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the manuscript and comparison to other symbioses.

claim: Aposymbiotic Aiptasia were fed Artemia brine shrimp comprising nearly only cholesterol.
source: Symbiont-free animals ('aposymbiotic') were fed Artemia brine shrimp comprising nearly only cholesterol (Tolosa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aiptasia strain F003 hosts Symbiodiniaceae strains SSA01 and SSB01.
source: Aiptasia strain F003 hosts Symbiodiniaceae strains SSA01 and SSB01 (Grawunder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Acropora digitifera endogenous Symbiodiniaceae are uncultured but closely related to the cultured strain CCMP2466.
source: Acropora digitifera endogenous Symbiodiniaceae are uncultured but closely related to the cultured strain CCMP2466 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on the molecular typing described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Symbiodiniaceae, like their dinoflagellate relatives, produce many sterols, including the unique gorgosterol with its unusual cyclopropyl group.
source: Symbiodiniaceae, like their dinoflagellate relatives, produce many sterols, including the unique gorgosterol with its unusual cyclopropyl group.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by the sterol profiling data.

claim: Resident Symbiodiniaceae in adult Acropora digitifera parental colonies were typed with the chloroplast ribosomal DNA subunit 23S marker (cp23S) and identified as Symbiodiniaceae Clade C1.
source: Resident Symbiodiniaceae in adult parental colonies were typed with the chloroplast ribosomal DNA subunit 23S marker (cp23S) as previously described (Grawunder et al., 2015): 10 bacterial clones were sequenced per coral colony and all were identical (GenBank Accession MK696595), identified by BLASTn to the nr NCBI database as Symbiodiniaceae Clade C1.
evidence: This is directly supported by the molecular typing described in the Materials and methods section.
